summary: This standards-track memo defines a MIB, a set of objects for network management, that describes a router's IP forwarding table. It updates RFC 1354 by recognizing that CIDR routes can share a network number yet have different masks. It was replaced by RFC 4292.

plainLanguage.summary: A standard form for asking a router to show its list of directions for where to send each packet.

questions: how do i query a router's routing table
what is the ip forwarding mib
how do routers use routing tables
subtitle: How network management systems query a router's routing decisions.

tldr.problem: Network administrators need a standard way to inspect a router's forwarding table to see which routes are installed and where packets will be sent.
tldr.mechanism: This MIB defines SNMP objects that let management stations query routing table entries, including support for Classless Inter-Domain Routing (CIDR) where multiple routes can share the same network number with different subnet masks.
tldr.outcome: Network operators gained a standard interface to monitor routing decisions; it was replaced by RFC 4292, which further refined the model.

today: RFC 2096 is Proposed Standard status and has been obsoleted by RFC 4292, which provides further refinement of the IP routing MIB. Implementations that support SNMP management of routing tables should use RFC 4292 instead.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
RFC 2096 defines the IP Forwarding Table MIB, a management information base for querying IP routing tables. It is an update to RFC 1354 to accommodate Classless Inter-Domain Routing (CIDR), which allows routers to have multiple routes to the same network address with different subnet masks.

The RFC acknowledges that earlier management models did not handle this case: when CIDR is used, the same destination network can appear with different masks, and they must be tracked separately. This MIB adds that support while maintaining backward compatibility.
sections.plainLanguage: This standard tells you how to ask a router about its delivery rules. The older version didn't handle a tricky case: when the same address can have multiple rules depending on the mask, which this fixes.

sections.title: The MIB Structure
sections.content:
The MIB consists of two main tables and global objects. The ipCidrRouteNumber object reports the count of active routing entries, allowing management stations to detect changes without reading the entire table.

The ipCidrRouteTable is the main routing table. Each entry represents a single route and includes the destination IP address, subnet mask, Type of Service (TOS) policy selector, and the next hop address. The table is indexed by these four values, meaning you can look up a specific route if you know where packets are going and which policy applies.

An older ipForwardTable is marked obsolete in this RFC; it did not support separate masks for the same destination network, so the CIDR table replaced it.
sections.plainLanguage: There's a counter that tells you how many routes are active. The main table lists every route: where packets should go, which subnet mask to use, what service level matters, and which neighbor to send them to first. An older table in the RFC is no longer used.

sections.title: Route Entry Fields
sections.content:
Each route entry in the ipCidrRouteTable includes these core fields:

ipCidrRouteDest is the destination IP address (the network prefix). ipCidrRouteMask is the subnet mask; when logically AND-ed with the destination, it must equal the destination—this prevents invalid prefix values.

ipCidrRouteTos encodes the IP Type of Service bits, allowing policy-based routing where the same destination may have different routes for different service classes. ipCidrRouteNextHop is the IP address of the next router on the path to the destination, or 0.0.0.0 for local routes.

ipCidrRouteIfIndex identifies which local network interface to use when sending to the next hop. ipCidrRouteType is one of four values: other (unspecified), reject (discard matching packets), local (the destination is directly reachable), or remote (forwarding to another router).
sections.plainLanguage: Each route record says: 'send packets to this address using this mask through that interface to reach this neighbor'. The router also marks whether it's a local delivery or a rejection.

sections.title: Routing Protocol Information
sections.content:
ipCidrRouteProto identifies the routing protocol that installed the route: static management, RIP, OSPF, BGP, and many others are listed. ipCidrRouteAge is the number of seconds since the route was last verified, helping detect stale entries.

ipCidrRouteNextHopAS is the autonomous system number of the next hop, used by exterior gateway protocols like BGP. Up to five ipCidrRouteMetric fields (1 through 5) hold routing metrics whose meaning depends on the protocol; if unused, they are set to -1.

ipCidrRouteInfo is an object identifier pointing to protocol-specific routing information, allowing extensions for details particular to each routing protocol. ipCidrRouteStatus controls whether the row is valid, using standard row status conventions for management station control of the routing table.
sections.plainLanguage: These fields tell you which routing protocol created the route, how old the information is, what metrics it uses (hop count, delay, etc.), and which system is next. Management stations can use these fields to add, update, or remove routes.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC states that security is not an objective in this MIB's view. It does not define any access controls or authentication mechanisms; those are expected to be provided by the SNMP framework itself (SNMPv2, SNMPv3, or the deployment's chosen security model).

Because routing tables directly control network forwarding, access to modify routing MIB objects should be restricted to authorized network administrators through the security mechanisms of the SNMP protocol. Read-only access may be safer for monitoring but exposes the network topology; deployment should consider the trade-off.
sections.plainLanguage: This MIB does not have built-in security; it relies on your SNMP security settings. Since changing routes can break the network, only trusted people should be able to modify them through this interface.
